title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine, but It Still Has Room to Open a New Front Against NATO
dek: Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry warfare experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity to launch a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.
why: The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief diplomatic correspondent and was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his judgments on Russian military capability and Europe's fractures are far more concrete than those of TV commentators.
who: People watching Eastern European geopolitics, energy and defense security, and foreign-policy readers trying to judge the real leverage in Russia-Ukraine negotiations.

points.h: Trump's anti-Europe talk may be taken literally by Putin
points.body: Everyone is guessing whether John Ratcliffe's secret trip to Russia was to negotiate terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit looks more like carrying a message from Trump to the Russian side: don't take those on-air remarks about ‘America not caring about Europe’ seriously — if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia or Finland, the US will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and badly needs to cut off European support for Ukraine, so escalating a probe against NATO is one option, while Trump's earlier statements such as ‘Europe is a bunch of freeloaders’ gave Putin room to misread, hence the need for a dedicated trip to make the red line clear. One caveat: the guest does not have intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why the account ‘makes complete sense’, not confirming it.

points.h: Russia's army isn't exhausted and can still open a limited front
points.body: Russia has been unable to take Ukraine for a long time — does that mean it cannot open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it can absolutely open a ‘limited front’ — not tanks rolling across Poland to Paris, but making trouble in the Baltic direction, for example blockading the narrow land corridor of the Suwalki Gap. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world today that fight modern drone-infantry warfare as a daily routine. The story of a 20-person Ukrainian drone team destroying an entire traditional battalion is widely told, but the Russian military has the same technology in hand: 20 Russians can likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that has not trained against drones. Outsiders assume Russia grows weaker the longer it fights, but overlook that it is also one of the parties tempered by this technological revolution.

points.h: NATO might not even rescue Lithuania from Poland
points.body: A war game designed to simulate a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not insufficient military power, but that Russian forces advance too fast and nuclear deterrence hangs over everything, so allies fall into hesitation over ‘whether to enter’, producing a chain of waiting and watching. The guest says Moscow has factored exactly this into its options. He also cautions that this is not quite the same as before 2022 — back then, hundreds of thousands of Russian troops massing could be clearly seen on the German and Belarusian borders, and there is no such material preparation now. So the most direct escalation may not be a conventional invasion, but rather small, ambiguous attacks that can be denied (hitting a warehouse or drones first).

points.h: Russia is using drones to test NATO's bottom line
points.body: At this stage, without the signal of a massed army on the border, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or using captured Ukrainian drones modified for the purpose to create an incident, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the US steps in. The guest notes such probing is already underway — an armed drone attacked a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented deaths; Russian risk-taking is steadily rising, and the West has so far given no serious response. The senior European officers he has spoken with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term — the Kremlin will want to act before the US might let go.

points.h: Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
points.body: Would Putin accept a decent ceasefire deal? The guest's view is that you only need to look at what is put on the table: Russia has consistently demanded not just territory, but a cap on the size of Ukraine's army, limits on weapons types, and cutting off Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, the goal is to make Ukraine ‘lose the ability to defend itself’; not neutral, but ‘castrated’, so that it cannot rise again in the next stage of war — a year, five years or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes the former Ukrainian foreign minister's summary: this war will end in only one of two outcomes — the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not an option.

points.h: Street protests can decide the fate of a wartime cabinet
points.body: Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: elections are frozen in wartime, and the president's legitimacy rests on just one ballast stone — ‘street support’. Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who drove drone innovation, because he needed the support of Commander-in-Chief Syrsky; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv elites took to the streets, and the protests, small in scale, were enough to make the president reverse course — he removed Syrsky, replaced him with a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with a veteran intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption bodies can still pursue people in the president's innermost circle, and when Zelensky tried to amend the law to absorb that body, he backed down within a week under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square equals the ballot box.

points.h: Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
points.body: Summing up Ukrainian perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what truly drives them. The guest says that after Russian troops take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is send bulldozers to tear down monuments to the victims of the 1930s famine — what they want to erase is a memory. Russian state television talks about how to ‘re-educate’ Ukrainians, making them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II, the Soviets carried out a systematic purge of Ukraine's cultural elite, and in the guest's childhood he had no idea those writers existed, because collective memory had been wiped out. Ukrainians today are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat grinder of history, carrying the trauma in their bodies; it is precisely the fear of ‘never again’ that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield rather than return to that life.

points.h: Half a million veterans blocked the first wave of collapse
points.body: On the night of February 23, 2022, most people in Kyiv still did not believe there would be war; the guest remembers knowing from his experience in Kabul and Baghdad that ‘impossible’ can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference point. What truly kept the country from collapsing in the first days was eight years of war in the Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it produced roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had traded blows with the Russian army, and volunteer organizations evolved into a flexible, aggressive force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in the Donbas — ‘we know what they look like, we know how to fight them’. Because of that experience, the swift collapse Putin expected did not happen, and the West's widespread expectations were wrong too.
